e: From Middle English atstonden, etstonden, ætstanden, from Old English ætstandan (“to stand still, stand at, stand near, stand in, stand by, stop, rest, stay, remain, stand up, check, resist, cease, blight (crops)”), equivalent to at- + stand. Conflated in some senses with Middle English anstanden (“to resist”). See astand.
From Middle English atstunten, etstunten, ætstunten, from Old English ætstyntan (“to blunt, dull, weaken”), equivalent to at- + stunt. See astint.
From Middle English atschoten, ætscheoten, from Old English ætscēotan (“to escape, disappear”), equivalent to at- + shoot. Compare Dutch ontschieten (“to slip from, forget”), German entschiessen.
From Middle English atsliken, ætsliken, equivalent to at- + slike. Compare German entschleichen.

Borrowed from Japanese 暑がり (atsugari, “one who dislikes hot temperature”), from 暑い (atsui, “hot”) + (verb-)がり (gari, “one who dislikes something”, literally “one often shows expression of something”).
From Middle English atslupen, etslupen, ætslupen, from Old English *ætslūpan (“to slip away”), equivalent to at- + slip. See aslip, aslope.
From Middle English atsitten, ætsitten, from Old English ætsittan (“to sit by, remain, stay, wait”), equivalent to at- + sit. See also asit.
From Middle English atscheaken, atsceken, equivalent to at- + shake. Compare ashake.
From Middle English atstutten, etstutten, ætstutten (“to tarry”), equivalent to at- + stut.
From Middle English atsaken, ætsaken, from Old English ætsacan (“to deny, disown, abjure, renounce”), equivalent to at- + sake.
Orthographic borrowing from Cebuano or Tagalog atsara. Doublet of atchara, acar, and acha(a)r(a).

q: "Ach sure, there's no harm in the one drink atself, but wasn't Mrs. Farrell telling us Father had an extra twelve last night after his tay?"

e: From Middle English atspringen, ætspringen, from Old English ætspringan (“to rush forth, spurt out, spring out”), equivalent to at- + spring. Compare Dutch ontspringen (“to spring, well, outflow”), German entspringen (“to spring from, escape, arise”).
From at- + scape (“to escape”), perhaps modelled after Middle English atscheaken ("to escape"; see atshake). More at ascape, escape.
